subject: Renal
subtopic: Nephritic syndrome: infection-related, IgA, RPGN, DPGN
vignette: A 6-year-old develops dark urine and facial swelling 3 weeks after an episode of streptococcal pharyngitis that was treated with antibiotics. Serum C3 is low, C4 is normal, and blood pressure is elevated. The physician diagnoses infection-related glomerulonephritis.
question: Which immunologic mechanism and timing are characteristic of this disease?

options.text: Type I hypersensitivity with immediate symptoms during the infection
Type IV hypersensitivity occurring months after the infection
Type III hypersensitivity with consumptive hypocomplementemia, typically 2–4 weeks after group A streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection
Anti-GBM antibody disease occurring concurrently with a respiratory infection
IgA deposition occurring simultaneously with a mucosal infection

explanation_correct: Infection-related, or post-streptococcal, glomerulonephritis is a type III hypersensitivity reaction in which immune complexes deposit in the glomerulus and consume complement, producing hypocomplementemia with low C3. In children it classically appears about 2 to 4 weeks after group A streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection, when the patient seems to be recovering. The latent period reflects the time needed for antibody and immune-complex formation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Type I hypersensitivity is immediate and IgE-mediated, as in anaphylaxis; it is not the mechanism of post-streptococcal GN, which has a latency of weeks.
explanation_incorrect.B: Type IV hypersensitivity is a delayed T-cell-mediated response, not the immune-complex mechanism here, and the typical interval is 2 to 4 weeks rather than months.
explanation_incorrect.D: Anti-GBM antibody disease (Goodpasture syndrome) is a type II hypersensitivity process and does not follow streptococcal infection with a latent period.
explanation_incorrect.E: IgA nephropathy occurs concurrently with respiratory or GI infections and does not feature consumptive hypocomplementemia after group A streptococcus.

educationalObjective: Infection-related GN is a type III hypersensitivity with consumptive hypocomplementemia, appearing 2–4 weeks after group A streptococcal infection.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Nephritic syndrome: infection-related, IgA, RPGN, DPGN
vignette: A renal biopsy from a 10-year-old with suspected post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is examined. Light microscopy shows enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with a granular 'starry sky' appearance. Immunofluorescence is positive for IgG, IgM, and C3 along the GBM and mesangium, and electron microscopy reveals electron-dense deposits on the subepithelial side of the GBM.
question: Which of the following best describes the immunofluorescence and electron-microscopic findings in this disease?

options.text: Granular 'lumpy-bumpy' deposition of IgG, IgM, and C3 along the GBM and mesangium with subepithelial immune-complex humps
Linear deposition of IgG along the GBM with no electron-dense deposits
Pauci-immune staining with no immunoglobulin or complement deposition
IgA-dominant mesangial deposits with mesangial proliferation
Granular subendothelial IgG and C3 with wire-loop thickening of capillaries

explanation_correct: Infection-related glomerulonephritis is characterized by granular, lumpy-bumpy immunofluorescence due to deposition of IgG, IgM, and C3 along the GBM and in the mesangium, corresponding to the starry-sky appearance on light microscopy. Electron microscopy shows the classic subepithelial immune-complex humps. These findings reflect immune-complex deposition, and in adults Staphylococcus aureus is an additional causative organism.

explanation_incorrect.B: Linear IgG along the GBM is the hallmark of anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease, not infection-related GN.
explanation_incorrect.C: Pauci-immune staining with no immune deposition is characteristic of ANCA-associated rapidly progressive GN, not post-infectious GN.
explanation_incorrect.D: Mesangial IgA deposits define IgA nephropathy, which occurs concurrently with mucosal infections rather than after streptococcal infection.
explanation_incorrect.E: Subendothelial IgG and C3 with wire-loop thickening describes diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis of SLE, not infection-related GN with subepithelial humps.

educationalObjective: Infection-related GN shows granular lumpy-bumpy IgG/IgM/C3 deposition with subepithelial humps on EM.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Nephritic syndrome: infection-related, IgA, RPGN, DPGN
vignette: A 19-year-old man develops cola-colored urine while recovering from a diarrheal illness. He has no recent streptococcal infection; symptoms began at the same time as the gastrointestinal illness. Serum complement is normal. Biopsy shows proliferation of mesangial cells, and immunofluorescence demonstrates IgA-based deposits in the mesangium.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Goodpasture syndrome
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis type II
Minimal change disease
IgA nephropathy (Berger disease)

explanation_correct: IgA nephropathy, or Berger disease, occurs concurrently with respiratory or gastrointestinal infections because IgA is secreted by mucosal linings. It is characterized by mesangial proliferation with IgA-based immune-complex deposits in the mesangium and hematuria. Normal complement and the simultaneous onset with a mucosal illness distinguish it from post-streptococcal GN. It is also the renal pathology of IgA vasculitis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Post-streptococcal GN appears 2 to 4 weeks after infection, has low C3, and shows subepithelial humps rather than mesangial IgA.
explanation_incorrect.B: Goodpasture syndrome is an anti-GBM disease with linear IgG, pulmonary hemorrhage, and no mesangial IgA deposits.
explanation_incorrect.C: MPGN type II is associated with C3 nephritic factor and intramembranous dense deposits, not mesangial IgA.
explanation_incorrect.D: Minimal change disease causes nephrotic syndrome with foot-process effacement and no mesangial IgA or hematuria.

educationalObjective: IgA nephropathy features concurrent mucosal infection, mesangial proliferation, and mesangial IgA deposits with normal complement.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Nephritic syndrome: infection-related, IgA, RPGN, DPGN
vignette: A 42-year-old man has rapidly worsening renal function over 2 weeks, with severe hypertension, hematuria, and RBC casts. Biopsy shows glomeruli with crescent-shaped masses occupying Bowman space, composed of fibrin, plasma proteins including C3b, glomerular parietal cells, monocytes, and macrophages.
question: Which of the following best characterizes these histologic findings?

options.text: Subepithelial humps with granular IgG deposition along the GBM
Crescentic glomerulonephritis with a poor prognosis
Diffuse wire-loop thickening with subendothelial immune deposits
Mesangial proliferation with dominant IgA deposition
Pure podocyte foot-process effacement with no inflammatory cells

explanation_correct: Rapidly progressive, or crescentic, glomerulonephritis is defined by crescent-shaped accumulations in Bowman space made of fibrin, plasma proteins such as C3b, glomerular parietal cells, monocytes, and macrophages. It is an aggressive nephritic syndrome with a poor prognosis and rapidly declining GFR. Underlying causes include anti-GBM disease, ANCA-associated vasculitis, and immune-complex diseases such as PSGN and DPGN.

explanation_incorrect.A: Subepithelial humps with granular IgG are characteristic of infection-related GN, not crescentic GN.
explanation_incorrect.C: Wire-loop subendothelial deposits describe diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis of SLE, which is not defined by crescents.
explanation_incorrect.D: Mesangial IgA deposition defines IgA nephropathy, not crescentic GN.
explanation_incorrect.E: Isolated foot-process effacement is the lesion of minimal change disease, without crescents or inflammatory cells.

educationalObjective: Crescentic (rapidly progressive) glomerulonephritis consists of fibrin/C3b, parietal cells, monocytes, and macrophages and carries a poor prognosis.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Nephritic syndrome: infection-related, IgA, RPGN, DPGN
vignette: A renal pathology laboratory reviews immunofluorescence patterns in four patients with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. The observed patterns include linear GBM staining, pauci-immune staining, and granular staining. The faculty member asks which patterns correspond to specific causes.
question: Which of the following correctly pairs immunofluorescence patterns with their underlying diseases?

options.text: Linear IgG — ANCA-associated granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Pauci-immune — anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease
Granular subepithelial — microscopic polyangiitis
Linear IgG — Goodpasture syndrome; pauci-immune — ANCA-associated vasculitis; granular — PSGN or DPGN
Mesangial IgA — membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis type II

explanation_correct: Immunofluorescence is central to classifying RPGN. Linear IgG reflecting antibodies against GBM and alveolar basement membrane defines Goodpasture syndrome, a type II hypersensitivity process. Pauci-immune disease, with no Ig or complement deposition, comprises the ANCA-associated vasculitides: granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and microscopic polyangiitis. Granular deposition is typical of immune-complex diseases such as PSGN and DPGN.

explanation_incorrect.A: GPA is pauci-immune with PR3/c-ANCA; linear IgG is the pattern of Goodpasture syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.B: Goodpasture disease shows linear IgG along the GBM, not a pauci-immune pattern.
explanation_incorrect.C: Microscopic polyangiitis is pauci-immune with MPO/p-ANCA; granular subepithelial staining belongs to infection-related GN.
explanation_incorrect.E: MPGN type II is associated with C3 nephritic factor and intramembranous dense deposits, not mesangial IgA, which is IgA nephropathy.

educationalObjective: RPGN immunofluorescence: linear = anti-GBM (Goodpasture), pauci-immune = ANCA vasculitis, granular = immune-complex GN (PSGN/DPGN).

subject: Renal
subtopic: Nephritic syndrome: infection-related, IgA, RPGN, DPGN
vignette: A 28-year-old man presents with hemoptysis and acute renal failure. Urinalysis shows hematuria and RBC casts. Renal biopsy shows crescents with necrosis and breaks in the GBM, and immunofluorescence demonstrates linear deposition of IgG along the glomerular basement membrane.
question: Which of the following best explains the combination of pulmonary and renal findings?

options.text: Type II hypersensitivity with antibodies against GBM and alveolar basement membrane (Goodpasture syndrome)
Type III hypersensitivity with circulating immune complexes depositing in lung and kidney
Pauci-immune ANCA-mediated injury to small vessels
IgA deposition in the renal mesangium and pulmonary mucosa
Subendothelial immune-complex deposition from systemic lupus erythematosus

explanation_correct: Goodpasture syndrome is a type II hypersensitivity disease in which antibodies target type IV collagen in both the glomerular basement membrane and the alveolar basement membrane. This produces the classic combination of hematuria, with RBC casts and crescents, and hemoptysis, with linear IgG deposition on immunofluorescence. The biopsy showing breaks in the GBM, necrosis, and crescent formation is consistent with this diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: A type III hypersensitivity mechanism with immune-complex deposition produces granular staining, as in PSGN or SLE, not the linear IgG seen here.
explanation_incorrect.C: ANCA-associated vasculitis is pauci-immune with no linear IgG deposition and does not feature anti-basement membrane antibodies.
explanation_incorrect.D: IgA nephropathy is a mesangial, hematuria-predominant disease triggered by mucosal infection; it does not cause pulmonary hemorrhage or linear IgG.
explanation_incorrect.E: SLE causes granular subendothelial IgG and C3 deposition with wire loops and is not characterized by linear anti-GBM antibodies.

educationalObjective: Goodpasture syndrome is a type II anti-GBM disease with linear IgG, hematuria, and hemoptysis from alveolar basement membrane involvement.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Nephritic syndrome: infection-related, IgA, RPGN, DPGN
vignette: A 55-year-old woman has rapidly progressive renal failure, hematuria, and sinusitis with pulmonary nodules. Biopsy shows necrotizing crescents with no significant immunoglobulin or complement deposition on immunofluorescence. Serum testing is positive for PR3-ANCA.
question: Which of the following best categorizes this patient's disease?

options.text: Goodpasture syndrome with linear anti-GBM antibodies
Infection-related GN with low complement
Pauci-immune granulomatosis with polyangiitis (c-ANCA/PR3), a cause of RPGN
IgA vasculitis with mesangial IgA deposition
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis type II with C3 nephritic factor

explanation_correct: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is one of the ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitides that cause pauci-immune rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. It is associated with c-ANCA targeting proteinase 3 and features upper and lower respiratory tract involvement, such as sinusitis and pulmonary nodules, alongside necrotizing glomerulonephritis. The absence of Ig and complement on immunofluorescence is the defining pauci-immune feature; related diseases include EGPA and MPA with p-ANCA/MPO.

explanation_incorrect.A: Goodpasture syndrome shows linear IgG on immunofluorescence and anti-GBM antibodies, not a pauci-immune pattern or PR3-ANCA.
explanation_incorrect.B: Infection-related GN has granular IgG and C3 deposition with consumptive hypocomplementemia, not pauci-immune crescents.
explanation_incorrect.D: IgA vasculitis deposits IgA in the mesangium and does not cause PR3-ANCA positivity or pauci-immune necrosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: MPGN type II is driven by C3 nephritic factor with intramembranous dense deposits, not pauci-immune crescents or PR3-ANCA.

educationalObjective: GPA causes pauci-immune RPGN with c-ANCA/PR3, respiratory involvement, and necrotizing crescents lacking immune deposits.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Nephritic syndrome: infection-related, IgA, RPGN, DPGN
vignette: A 22-year-old woman with known systemic lupus erythematosus develops nephrotic-range proteinuria, hematuria, and rising creatinine. Renal biopsy shows thickened capillary loops with a 'wire-loop' appearance. Immunofluorescence is granular for IgG and C3 in a subendothelial distribution.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and its typical presentation?

options.text: IgA nephropathy with mesangial IgA and concurrent infection
Infection-related GN with subepithelial humps and low C3
Goodpasture syndrome with linear IgG and hemoptysis
MPGN type II with intramembranous dense deposits and C3 nephritic factor
Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (lupus nephritis) with wire loops and granular subendothelial IgG/C3, often presenting as nephritic-nephrotic syndrome

explanation_correct: Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis is the severe form of lupus nephritis, often called wire lupus because of the wire-loop thickening of capillary loops on light microscopy. Immunofluorescence shows granular deposition of IgG, often with C3, in subendothelial locations, sometimes with subepithelial or intramembranous deposits. DPGN and MPGN frequently present with combined nephritic and nephrotic features, or nephritic-nephrotic syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.A: IgA nephropathy shows mesangial IgA deposits and hematuria concurrent with mucosal infection, not wire loops with subendothelial IgG.
explanation_incorrect.B: Infection-related GN shows subepithelial humps, not subendothelial wire-loop deposits, and follows streptococcal infection.
explanation_incorrect.C: Goodpasture syndrome has linear anti-GBM IgG with pulmonary hemorrhage rather than granular lupus deposits.
explanation_incorrect.D: MPGN type II features intramembranous dense deposits with C3 nephritic factor and tram-track GBM splitting, not the wire-loop IgG pattern of lupus.

educationalObjective: DPGN (lupus nephritis) shows wire-loop capillary thickening with granular subendothelial IgG/C3 and often causes nephritic-nephrotic syndrome.
